title: Trade-offs & Evolution
scopeHtml: Scope: communicating architecture decisions, spotting over/under-engineering, migrating under live traffic, team scaling, legacy rescue, incremental adoption, build-vs-buy, tech debt, and the "design your app architecture" interview.

questions.promptHtml: What is an Architecture Decision Record, and why would you write one for an Android app?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors are expected to leave a paper trail so decisions survive attrition and re-litigation. Checks if you can separate "what we chose" from "why".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An ADR is a short, immutable, version-controlled note capturing one significant decision: context, the decision, alternatives, and consequences. I write one when a choice is expensive to reverse, like Hilt vs Koin, multi-module layout, or MVI vs MVVM. Six months later a new hire or I can read why we chose it and whether the original constraints still hold.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Michael Nygard's classic format has Title, Status (proposed / accepted / superseded), Context, Decision, Consequences. MADR extends it with explicit "considered options" and decision drivers (Nygard's original does not force you to list rejected alternatives, which is a common gap).

docs/adr/
  0007-use-hilt-for-di.md        Status: Accepted
  0012-feature-modules-by-domain.md  Status: Accepted
  0019-replace-rxjava-with-flow.md   Status: Proposed
  0007 later => "Superseded by 0031" (never edit history, supersede it)

Rules that make ADRs useful: one decision per file; store in the repo and review via PR (the PR thread is the debate); record the constraints (team size, deadline, min SDK) because decisions are only right relative to constraints; always include negative consequences.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
(a minimal record)

# 0012. Split features into :feature:* modules
Status: Accepted (2025-03-04)
Context: 14 devs, 1 app module, clean build 11 min, merge conflicts daily.
Decision: One module per user-facing domain; :core:* for shared infra.
Options: keep monolith + build cache; modules by layer (:ui,:data).
Consequences: + parallel builds, ownership. - boilerplate, navigation wiring, 2 sprints of migration.
Revisit when: build time < 4 min or team < 6.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing ADRs after the fact as justification; no alternatives listed.
  • Editing old ADRs instead of superseding them, losing history.
  • Documenting trivial choices (naming) so nobody reads the folder.
  • No "revisit when" trigger, so stale decisions persist.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you store them? → In the repo next to code, reviewed through PRs.
  2. How do you handle a decision that turned out wrong? → New ADR with Status superseding the old one, linking both.
  3. How do you stop ADRs becoming bureaucracy? → Only for hard-to-reverse decisions, half a page, written by the person proposing the change.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "documentation of decisions." Senior: ties ADRs to reversibility, records constraints and exit criteria, and uses the PR as the debate record.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team re-debated "why not Koin" every time a new lead joined; one ADR with the original startup-time and compile-safety constraints ended it in a single review.

questions.promptHtml: How do you tell whether an Android codebase is over-engineered or under-engineered?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Both failure modes are common; seniors calibrate architecture to team size and product stage rather than defaulting to "more layers".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I look at the cost of a typical change. If adding a text field touches eight files across four layers with pass-through mappers, it's over-engineered. If a one-line change breaks unrelated screens, you can't test a ViewModel without a device, or two people can't edit the same package without conflicts, it's under-engineered. Architecture should be sized to current pain plus the next 12 months, not an imagined future.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Signal Over-engineered Under-engineered
Typical change Many files, trivial logic Few files, wide blast radius
Layers Use case that only calls repo.get() Business logic in Activity/Fragment
Modules 80 modules for 6 devs, each with 3 classes One :app module, 11 min builds
Abstractions Interface with one implementation, never faked Singletons reached statically, untestable
Mappers DTO -> Entity -> Domain -> UiModel with identical fields Network DTO used in composables
Tests Mock-heavy, coupled to structure None, or only UI tests

Test of a layer: "what would I lose if I deleted it?" If nothing but a hop, delete it. Test of a missing layer: "can I change X without touching Y?"

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Over-engineered: a use case that adds nothing
class GetUserUseCase @Inject constructor(private val repo: UserRepository) {
    operator fun invoke(id: String) = repo.getUser(id)
}
// Justified: combines sources and encodes a rule reused by 2+ screens
class GetFeedUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val posts: PostRepository, private val blocked: BlockRepository,
) {
    operator fun invoke(): Flow<List<Post>> =
        combine(posts.feed(), blocked.ids()) { p, b -> p.filter { it.authorId !in b } }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Copying a big-company reference architecture onto a 4-person app.
  • Treating "no architecture" as speed; it is borrowed time with interest.
  • Measuring by file count instead of change cost.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What would you do on a 3-person startup app? → Single module, ViewModel + repository, Hilt or manual DI, split only when builds or conflicts hurt.
  2. How do you measure change cost? → Files touched per PR, PR cycle time, lead time for changes.
  3. When do you add a domain layer? → When logic is shared across ViewModels or is complex enough to unit-test in isolation (the official guide calls it optional).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists patterns they know. Senior frames it as cost-of-change and team-size fit, with measurable signals and deletion as a valid refactor.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: One app had a 6-layer "clean" stack; a new filter chip took 3 days. Collapsing pass-through use cases and mappers cut typical PRs from 14 files to 5.

questions.promptHtml: What is the real cost of an abstraction (interface, mapper, wrapper) in an Android app, and when is it worth paying?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you reason about abstraction as a purchase with ongoing cost, not a virtue.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Every abstraction costs reading indirection, boilerplate, onboarding time, and sometimes build time or runtime. It pays off when it isolates something that changes independently, enables a test seam you actually use, or protects a boundary like network or storage. I wrap volatile or vendor-owned things, and I don't wrap stable things I control.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Costs: (1) cognitive, jump-to-definition lands on an interface; (2) mechanical, mappers and bindings (@Binds) per type; (3) build, more modules/kapt-ksp output; (4) runtime, extra allocations in hot paths such as per-item mapping on 10k-row lists; (5) leaky abstraction risk, where the interface mirrors one vendor's API so it isn't a real abstraction.

Worth paying when:

  • A dependency is volatile (analytics SDK, payment SDK, feature-flag vendor).
  • The seam is used by tests (fakes beat mocks).
  • It enforces a dependency direction (domain must not know Retrofit).
  • Multiple implementations exist now (not "someday").

Rule of three: abstract on the second or third real use, not the first.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Worth it: vendor SDK behind a narrow, app-shaped interface
interface Analytics { fun track(event: AppEvent) }
class FirebaseAnalytics @Inject constructor(private val fa: com.google.firebase.analytics.FirebaseAnalytics) : Analytics {
    override fun track(event: AppEvent) = fa.logEvent(event.name, event.params.toBundle())
}
// Not worth it: wrapper that re-exposes the library
interface MyRetrofit { fun <T> create(c: Class<T>): T }  // zero value

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• One-implementation interfaces "for testing" when the class could simply be faked via constructor injection of its collaborators.
  • Domain models identical to DTOs plus a mapper both ways.
  • Wrapping Room DAOs in a data-source interface nobody swaps.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Fakes or mocks? → Fakes for stateful collaborators; mocks make tests brittle and structure-coupled.
  2. How do you decide on mappers? → Map at a boundary when shapes or lifetimes differ (wire format vs UI); skip when identical.
  3. How do you remove an abstraction safely? → Inline via IDE refactor, one module at a time, with tests green.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "abstraction = good practice, depend on interfaces." Senior: prices it, applies the rule of three, wraps volatile vendors, and deletes dead seams.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An SDK swap of the analytics vendor took 2 days because only one wrapper class changed; the same team spent weeks maintaining 40 never-swapped repository interfaces.

questions.promptHtml: How do you decide between building something in-house and adopting a third-party library in an Android app?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Dependency choices are long-lived architectural decisions; juniors add libraries by Stack Overflow popularity.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I score the library on fit, maintenance health, size/method cost, transitive dependencies, license, and exit cost. If it's non-differentiating (image loading, networking, DI) I buy. If it's core to our product or the library would dominate our code and is hard to leave, I either build or put it behind a thin seam. I always know how I'd remove it before I add it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Checklist:

  • Maintenance: last release, open issue response, bus factor, Kotlin/AGP compatibility (does it keep pace with AGP 8.x and Kotlin 2.x?).
  • Footprint: APK/AAB size impact, method count, R8 rules, transitive versions that clash with your catalog.
  • Architecture fit: KMP support, coroutine/Flow support, Compose support, threading model.
  • Lock-in: does its type leak into your domain or UI (e.g. Moshi annotations on domain models)? Leaks raise exit cost.
  • Security/licensing: license compatibility, CVE history, supply chain.
  • Build cost: KAPT-based libraries slow builds; prefer KSP-based ones where available.

Decision heuristic: buy commodity, build differentiator, wrap volatile. First-party Jetpack libraries are the default because they track platform changes.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// version catalog entry makes the cost visible and single-sourced
// libs.versions.toml
// coil = "3.x"   # verify current version before pinning
// dependencies { implementation(libs.coil.compose) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding a 300 KB library for one 20-line utility.
  • Choosing an abandoned library because it has 20k stars.
  • Letting library types spread through the whole app.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A library is archived upstream; what now? → Assess blast radius, fork only if small, else plan migration behind a seam with a deadline.
  2. Build in-house a custom image loader? → No, unless a measured need; Coil/Glide are commodity.
  3. How do you stop dependency sprawl? → Version catalog, a dependency-approval note (ADR) for new libraries, periodic review with dependencies reports.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE picks by popularity and features. Senior weighs ownership cost over 3 years and exit strategy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A popular animation library stopped releasing; with Lottie-like usage isolated in one module the team replaced it in a sprint, whereas a competing app scattered its types across 90 files.

questions.promptHtml: In an interview you are asked, "Design the architecture for our Android app." How do you approach it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: An open prompt reveals whether you gather requirements and reason about constraints before naming patterns.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I don't start with MVVM. I clarify product scope, scale, team size, offline needs, and constraints, then sketch layers and data flow, then module boundaries only if the team size justifies it, then cross-cutting concerns (DI, navigation, error handling, testing, observability), and I finish by naming the trade-offs and how it would evolve.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A repeatable frame (about 35 minutes):

1 Clarify (5m): users, DAU, offline?, real-time?, team size, min SDK, release cadence, existing code
2 Principles (2m): UDF, single source of truth, testability, ownership
3 Layers & data flow (10m): UI (Compose + ViewModel + UiState) -> optional domain -> repository -> local (Room) + remote
4 Modules (5m): by feature + :core; skip if <6 devs
5 Cross-cutting (8m): DI, navigation, error model, auth/session, config/feature flags, logging, analytics
6 Quality (3m): tests pyramid, CI, baseline profiles, crash/ANR monitoring
7 Trade-offs & evolution (2m): what I'd change at 10x users/devs

The unspoken grading: do you ask first, do you say "it depends" and then commit, do you flag risks (process death, config changes, offline sync conflicts), and do you size the solution to the team.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
(the skeleton you can draw)

data class FeedUiState(val items: List<Post> = emptyList(), val loading: Boolean = false, val error: UiError? = null)

class FeedViewModel @Inject constructor(private val repo: FeedRepository) : ViewModel() {
    val state: StateFlow<FeedUiState> = repo.feed()
        .map { FeedUiState(items = it) }
        .catch { emit(FeedUiState(error = it.toUiError())) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), FeedUiState(loading = true))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Jumping to "Clean Architecture with 7 modules" for an unknown app.
  • Ignoring offline/error/process death.
  • No mention of how you'd test or ship it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. 5 devs vs 50 devs? → Single module vs feature modules with ownership and convention plugins.
  2. What if backend is unstable? → Offline-first with Room as source of truth, retries, idempotent writes.
  3. How do you evolve it? → ADRs, incremental extraction, architecture tests (Konsist/lint) to protect boundaries.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE recites MVVM/Clean layers. Senior asks, sizes, orders decisions by reversibility, and calls out what is deliberately not built.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Candidates who asked "how many engineers and what's the release cadence?" first consistently proposed simpler, better-fitting designs.

questions.promptHtml: What is the strangler fig pattern, and how does it apply to migrating a mobile app's architecture?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Mobile can't do a big-bang rewrite: you can't roll back an installed binary instantly, so incremental migration matters.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Instead of rewriting, I build the new implementation around the old one and route more traffic to it screen by screen or feature by feature, until the old code has no callers and I delete it. On mobile I control the routing with a seam plus remote feature flags, so I can ramp up and roll back without a store release.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Martin Fowler notes the pattern is well known server-side but rarely applied to mobile. Mobile-specific constraints: binaries ship on store review cycles, users stay on old versions for months, and you can't hot-roll back code, only flags.

Phase 0: introduce seam        Caller -> Facade(interface) -> OldImpl
Phase 1: add NewImpl           Facade -> flag? NewImpl : OldImpl   (1% -> 10% -> 50%)
Phase 2: parallel run/shadow   run both, compare, log diffs
Phase 3: 100% on NewImpl       keep OldImpl behind flag one release
Phase 4: delete OldImpl + flag

Key rules: always ship a seam first (behavior-neutral); keep each step releasable; set a delete date for the flag, or you accumulate permanent dual paths (the most common failure).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface ProfileRepository { suspend fun load(id: String): Profile }

class SwitchingProfileRepository @Inject constructor(
    private val old: LegacyProfileRepository,
    private val new: NewProfileRepository,
    private val flags: FeatureFlags,
) : ProfileRepository {
    override suspend fun load(id: String) =
        if (flags.isOn("new_profile_repo")) new.load(id) else old.load(id)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Flags that never get removed.
  • Migrating the hardest screen first.
  • No metric defined to decide ramp-up or rollback.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the flag service is down? → Cached last-known value with safe default to old path.
  2. Data schema changes? → Expand/contract migrations; both versions must read the same store during the overlap.
  3. How do you prove equivalence? → Parallel run with diff logging before switching users.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "migrate gradually." Senior: seam first, flag ramp with guardrail metrics, version-skew awareness, and a deletion deadline.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that skipped the seam and rewrote checkout directly saw a 0.6% crash-free drop and needed a hotfix release (store delay of 2 days) because there was no kill switch.

questions.promptHtml: How do Conway's law and team structure influence your Android module design?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Architecture at scale is socio-technical; seniors design modules and teams together.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Conway's law says systems mirror the communication structure of the organization that builds them. So I align module boundaries with team ownership: each feature module has one owning team, shared :core modules have a platform owner, and dependencies between modules mirror allowed team dependencies. If I fight the org chart, I'll get a shared "misc" module that everyone edits and nobody owns.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Team Topologies describes stream-aligned teams (own a user journey end-to-end), platform teams (provide :core, build tooling), enabling teams, and complicated-subsystem teams. Mapping:

Stream team Feed     -> :feature:feed (+ :feature:feed:api if others need it)
Stream team Checkout -> :feature:checkout
Platform team        -> :core:network, :core:designsystem, build-logic/
Rule: feature modules never depend on each other's impl; talk via :api modules or navigation contracts

Mechanisms to make ownership real: CODEOWNERS per module, a module-owner file, CI rule that a new module needs an owner, api/impl split so a team's internals aren't consumed by others. Warning signs: a :common/:utils module with 30 authors, PRs needing 4 team approvals, cyclic feature dependencies (which mirror two teams that can't agree on a boundary).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# CODEOWNERS
/feature/feed/        @org/feed-team
/feature/checkout/    @org/checkout-team
/core/                @org/android-platform
/build-logic/         @org/android-platform

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Splitting by technical layer (:ui, :data) so every feature change crosses all teams.
  • Reorgs that don't move code ownership, leaving orphaned modules.
  • Over-modularizing for a team of 5.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Two teams need the same screen? → Extract to an owned shared module or one owns it and exposes an API; avoid co-ownership.
  2. Inverse Conway? → Shape the team structure to produce the architecture you want.
  3. How do you stop cross-team coupling creeping in? → Dependency rules enforced via Gradle api/impl visibility, lint or Konsist architecture tests.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "modules help build times." Senior: modules encode ownership and coordination cost; designs the boundary and the CODEOWNERS together.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A :shared module touched by 11 teams caused weekly merge conflicts; splitting it by owning team cut cross-team PR reviews by roughly half.

questions.contextHtml: A 9-year-old app (1.8M MAU, 220 screens, mixed Java/Kotlin) uses a hand-rolled ServiceLocator object plus some Dagger 2 components written by a former team. Cold start p50 is 1.9 s. Tests are hard: ServiceLocator.get<Api>() is called inside 1,400 classes. Management wants Hilt "by next quarter" but 12 feature squads ship every two weeks and nobody can freeze the codebase. A first attempt converting Application and 40 Activities in one PR was reverted after a crash spike: UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property repo has not been initialized in Fragments created by old code paths.
questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate to Hilt without stopping feature work?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Annotate everything with @AndroidEntryPoint and replace the locator in one big PR." Fails because Hilt requires an entire host chain (Activity -> Fragment) to be annotated, and a big bang can't be reviewed or rolled back.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which entry points are created outside Android's control (WorkManager, ContentProviders, services)? Is the existing Dagger graph worth keeping? What are the min SDK and build time budgets? Who owns each module? Are Java classes in scope (Hilt supports them)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep the reverted state; the old locator keeps working. Nothing ships half-converted.
  3. Hypotheses for the crash, ranked: (a) A Fragment annotated @AndroidEntryPoint hosted by an Activity that isn't (Hilt requires the host to be annotated too); (b) injected property accessed before super.onCreate/onAttach completes; (c) test or manual instantiation of the class bypassing injection; (d) multi-process component not initialised.
  4. How I'd verify: Reproduce with the stack trace, read the Hilt error output at build time (the host-annotation rule is a compile/runtime check), inspect the generated Hilt_* base classes, and write an instrumented smoke test per entry path.
  5. Root cause: Partial conversion of a host chain; injection happens in onAttach of Hilt_* generated superclass, which never ran for the unconverted parent chain.
  6. Fix: Strangle it in vertical slices.
    • Step 0: add Hilt to Application only, @HiltAndroidApp, with the legacy locator exposed as a Hilt @Module (@Provides fun api() = ServiceLocator.get<Api>()). Now both worlds see the same instances.
    • Step 1: migrate one screen as a whole chain (Activity + Fragments + ViewModel via @HiltViewModel), behind no flag, since it's a pure DI change; ship.
    • Step 2: new code only uses constructor injection; a lint/Detekt rule bans new ServiceLocator.get calls.
    • Step 3: invert module providers: move each Provides from the locator into Hilt modules and delete locator entries as consumers disappear.
    • Existing Dagger components: bridge with @EntryPoint or convert module by module; don't run two long-term graphs.
  7. Prevention: Per-slice instrumented smoke tests, a lint rule, a burn-down chart of ServiceLocator.get call sites (1,400 -> 0), crash-free monitoring per release.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No big-bang. No Koin swap in the middle (two migrations at once). Accept temporary dual wiring in exchange for shippability. Hilt adds KSP/KAPT build cost; use KSP where supported (verify Hilt/Dagger version).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Some code is Java-only and shared with another app? → Hilt supports Java; keep constructor injection plain @Inject so it also works with manual DI.
  • A ContentProvider needs deps before Application.onCreate? → Use @EntryPoint with EntryPointAccessors; avoid heavy work there.
  • Leadership wants a deadline? → Burn-down of call sites with a per-squad quota, not a date for "done".

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team converted 30 screens per sprint by making "touch a screen, convert its DI" part of the definition of done; the last 5% (WorkManager workers) took as long as the first 50% because of custom factories.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big-bang PR, no rollback thought, ignores host-annotation rule.
  • Hire: vertical slices, bridge module, lint ban on new locator calls.
  • Strong hire: burn-down metric, entry-point edge cases, avoids parallel migrations, quantifies build cost.

questions.promptHtml: How do you evaluate Now in Android (NiA) or similar reference apps as a model for your own app?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who cargo-cult a sample app lack judgment; seniors extract principles and discard context-specific parts.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: NiA is a teaching artifact: it demonstrates Google's recommended practices, optimized for showing many techniques and for a small team with a stable backend. I borrow the principles (UDF, offline-first source of truth, repository boundary, convention plugins, testing with fakes) and ask whether its structure fits my team size, domain complexity, and release process before adopting its module shape.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
What transfers well: offline-first with Room as single source of truth; StateFlow UI state; fakes instead of mocks; build-logic convention plugins and version catalogs; a testing strategy; separating :core:* and :feature:*; the api/impl split for feature modules (verify current repo state, it evolves).

What to question:

  • Module count and granularity: tuned to demonstrate modularization; your 6-dev app may not need it.
  • Optional domain layer: official guidance says it is optional; NiA added use cases only where logic was shared. Copying them wholesale yields pass-through use cases.
  • Backend assumptions: NiA uses a fake/static backend, hiding real concerns: auth, retries, pagination, schema drift, push.
  • Scale gaps: no multi-team ownership, no feature flags/experiments, limited observability, no large-list performance profile.

Evaluation method: list your top 5 pains; check if the reference solves them; adopt that part only; record in an ADR what you copied and why.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Principle worth copying: repository exposes a Flow from the local source of truth
class OfflineFirstTopicsRepository @Inject constructor(
    private val dao: TopicDao, private val network: TopicApi,
) : TopicsRepository {
    override fun topics(): Flow<List<Topic>> = dao.observeAll().map { it.map(TopicEntity::asModel) }
    suspend fun sync() { dao.upsert(network.fetch().map { it.asEntity() }) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating the sample as a standard rather than guidance.
  • Copying module granularity without the team size that justifies it.
  • Ignoring that the sample is updated; yesterday's pattern may be superseded (check release notes).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does NiA's approach scale to 100 engineers? → Principles do, structure needs ownership rules, flags, and build investment it doesn't show.
  2. Where does it fall short for a payment app? → Idempotency, security, strong consistency, audit logs.
  3. How would you document adoption? → ADR listing adopted/rejected parts with reasons.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE mirrors the folder structure. Senior extracts principles, maps to own constraints, and records what was deliberately not adopted.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that cloned NiA's module layout for a 4-dev app spent two sprints on wiring; they later merged 15 modules into 5 with no loss of test isolation.

questions.promptHtml: How do you identify, prioritize and pay down technical debt in an Android codebase while still shipping features?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can convert vague "the code is bad" into business-justified, sequenced work.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I treat debt as a loan with interest, and I pay down only debt that charges interest on code we change often. I measure interest by incident rate, change lead time, and build/CI cost in specific areas, rank by interest times change frequency, and fund it as a steady percentage of capacity plus opportunistic "leave it better" work, not a mythical refactor quarter.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Classify: deliberate vs accidental, and by interest. A hot module with high churn and many crashes is high-interest; an ugly stable class nobody touches is not.

Prioritization sketch:

score = churn(commits/90d) x defect rate x blast radius / cost to fix
Sources: git log churn, Crashlytics per-class, flaky test list, build scan hot spots

Funding patterns: ~15-20% capacity (calibrate; verify with your team), tie refactors to feature work in the same area, and make cleanup visible via a debt register with owners. Safety first: characterization tests before touching legacy code, then refactor in small steps, each releasable.

Communicate in business terms: "Checkout changes take 3x longer than average and caused 2 of 3 P1s; fixing X reduces lead time by an estimated 30%". Avoid "it's ugly".

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Characterization test: pins current behaviour before refactor
@Test fun `legacy discount rounds half up`() {
    assertEquals(Money(1005), LegacyPricing.applyDiscount(Money(1117), pct = 10))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Big-bang rewrite proposals with no incremental value.
  • Paying debt in untouched areas because it offends taste.
  • No metric to show payoff, so the budget disappears.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. PM refuses refactor time? → Bundle with a feature in that area, show incident/lead-time numbers.
  2. Rewrite vs refactor? → Refactor by default; rewrite only with strangler seams and bounded scope.
  3. How do you prevent new debt? → Lint/arch tests, PR checklist, ADRs, definition of done including tests.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "we should refactor X." Senior: quantifies interest, sequences by churn, funds continuously, and proves the result.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Hotspot analysis (churn x crashes) found 3 files accounting for 40% of crashes; targeted work there cut crash rate more than a months-long global cleanup would have.

questions.contextHtml: A news app (800k DAU, 90 screens, XML + Fragments + Navigation component, minSdk 24) wants Compose. Product refuses a feature freeze. After a pilot, the team reports: the first Compose screen shows 220 ms slower first frame in a list-in-Fragment due to nested scrolling inside a NestedScrollView; a ComposeView in a RecyclerView item flickers state on scroll; and java.lang.IllegalStateException: ViewTreeLifecycleOwner not found from androidx.compose.ui.platform.ComposeView crashed 0.4% of sessions in a dialog host. The tech lead proposes rewriting all 90 screens in two quarters.
questions.promptHtml: Plan the migration and explain how you would handle the three issues.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rewrite everything in Compose over two quarters." No risk ramp, ignores interop pitfalls and the fact that Navigation stays Fragment-based until the last Fragment is gone.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the design system shared (do we have XML styles to mirror in a Compose theme)? Which screens have highest change frequency? What's the Compose-literate headcount? Any hardware-heavy low-end device share? Baseline Profile support in CI?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the dialog screen's Compose variant via flag; fix the 0.4% crash.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Dialog/Window hosts not setting ViewTree owners: Dialogs create their own window; owners must be set on the dialog's decor view (or use DialogFragment which AndroidX handles). (b) RecyclerView item flicker: composition strategy disposing on detach; use ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed, hoist state out of the item, key stably. (c) Slow first frame: nested scroll containers measure infinite constraints; remove the wrapping NestedScrollView; add Baseline Profiles; check release build (never judge Compose perf in debug).
  4. How I'd verify: Reproduce with the stack trace; Layout Inspector for tree ownership; Perfetto/JankStats frame traces; Macrobenchmark with and without Baseline Profile on a low-end device.
  5. Root cause: Composition outside a proper ViewTree lifecycle owner, plus constraint and scroll nesting mismatches inherited from the View hierarchy.
  6. Fix & plan: Follow the official guidance: Compose and Views coexist; start with new screens, then migrate existing ones. Order: (1) shared design system as Compose theme mirroring XML tokens; (2) new screens in Compose with ComposeView in Fragments; (3) leaf components inside existing screens (bottom-up); (4) low-risk, high-churn screens; (5) migrate navigation last: keep Fragment navigation until all destinations are composables, then move to Navigation Compose.
  7. Prevention: Interop test checklist (dialogs, RecyclerView, process death), Compose compiler metrics for stability, Macrobenchmark gate in CI, lint for ComposeView without composition strategy.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No two-quarter rewrite; screens that rarely change stay in Views. Interop code is temporary cost; track it and delete it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Third-party View libraries without Compose equivalents? → Wrap in AndroidView; accept it.
  • APK size jump? → Compose adds runtime size; measure with R8 and compare; verify numbers per release.
  • Team unfamiliar with Compose? → Pair, a small component library, code review guild.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team migrated the 20 highest-churn screens first and left 40 legacy ones untouched for a year; productivity on the touched area rose, and the remainder was never worth the cost.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: rewrite-all plan.
  • Hire: incremental, bottom-up/new-screen-first, design system first, knows ViewTree owner issue.
  • Strong hire: metrics gates, navigation-last, accepts permanently-legacy screens, benchmarks release builds.

questions.contextHtml: A fintech app (2.4M MAU) is replacing its hand-written SQLite + Gson cache layer with Room + kotlinx.serialization. The transaction-history screen shows balances; a wrong number is a P0. Historic data is 80 MB for power users (about 150k rows). Engineering wants to ship the new layer behind a 10% flag. QA found that the new read path returns a subtotal differing by 1 cent in 0.03% of accounts, because the old path stored amounts as Double and the new one as Long minor units. Cold-start migration of the DB on a mid-range device took 4.8 s on the main thread in testing.
questions.promptHtml: How do you roll this out safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Flag at 10% and watch crashes." Crash metrics won't catch silent wrong numbers; also the migration blocks startup.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the source of truth (server)? Can the cache be rebuilt from the network? What's the acceptable tolerance for display differences? Is the DB shared across processes? Min SDK and storage constraints?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hold ramp at 0% user-visible; the new path runs in shadow only.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Double rounding (0.1+0.2 style) vs exact minor units; the old values are the wrong ones. (b) Locale/currency scale differences (JPY has 0 decimals). (c) Sort or filter semantics differences. (d) Startup jank from running the copy on the main thread.
  4. How I'd verify: Shadow reads: compute both, compare, log hashed diffs plus counts (no PII) to analytics; reproduce with the 1-cent accounts; StrictMode and Perfetto for main-thread I/O; test migration on a low-end device with 150k rows.
  5. Root cause: Floating-point legacy storage; the new layer is arguably right, but the visible number changes.
  6. Fix: Rollout in phases: (1) write path dual-writes old + new; (2) shadow read compare with 0% users seeing new output, until diff rate is understood; (3) agree with product on which number is canonical, ideally server-provided; (4) migrate data in a background WorkManager job in chunks (e.g. 5k rows/transaction) with resume support, never on the main thread; (5) ramp 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with guardrail metrics (diff rate, ANR, DB open time); (6) keep old tables one release for rollback, then drop.
  7. Prevention: Money as minor units + currency in the type system; migration tests with MigrationTestHelper; golden-dataset tests; kill switch; dashboards for diff rate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Dual-write doubles write cost and complexity temporarily; accepted for safety. I wouldn't ramp on crash metrics alone, and I wouldn't ship a destructive migration (no downgrade path) without a backup copy.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• User downgrades the app? → Room can't downgrade without a destructive fallback; keep the old DB file untouched until cleanup release.
  • Disk full during copy? → Transactional chunks, detect SQLiteFullException, retry later, stay on old path.
  • Shadow reads slow the UI? → Run on Dispatchers.IO off the critical path, sample 5% of reads.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found via shadow reads that 0.8% of rows had been silently truncated by the old serializer for years; the "bug" in the new path was the old one being wrong, and the fix needed a customer-support note.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flag + crash monitoring only.
  • Hire: shadow/dual path, background chunked migration, rollback plan.
  • Strong hire: defines canonical truth, diff telemetry without PII, money typing, version-skew/downgrade handling.

questions.contextHtml: You join as the first senior Android hire at a 7-year-old marketplace app: 1 module, 420k lines, 6 Activities holding 3,000-line onCreate logic, static singletons, an AsyncTask-era networking layer, 11% unit-test coverage, 3.1% ANR rate in Play vitals (bad-behavior threshold is 0.47%, verify current), crash-free sessions 98.2%. Releases are monthly and take 4 days of manual QA. The CEO says "fix quality, but don't stop features." You have 8 engineers and no architecture docs.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do in your first 90 days?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Propose a full rewrite in Compose with Clean Architecture." No data, no sequencing, no risk handling, and months of zero delivered value.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which journeys earn revenue? Where do ANRs/crashes cluster? Who knows the code best (bus factor)? What are the release constraints and QA process? What's the product roadmap for the next 2 quarters?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the biggest bleeding: top 3 ANR sources from Play vitals (main-thread I/O via StrictMode, broadcast receivers, SharedPreferences.commit()), shipped as small fixes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Main-thread disk/network in Activity lifecycle; (b) lock contention on singletons; (c) heavy Application.onCreate init; (d) layout over-inflation. Evidence beats guesses.
  4. How I'd verify: Play vitals ANR clusters, Perfetto/System trace, StrictMode in debug, Firebase/Sentry breadcrumbs, git log churn plus crash-per-class hotspot map.
  5. Root cause (typical): No seams, so everything blocks on the main thread and nothing is testable.
  6. Fix: Days 0-30 observe and stabilize: crash/ANR dashboards, CI with lint and a smoke test, fix top ANRs, release train automation. Days 30-60: characterization tests on the revenue journeys, introduce DI via incremental Hilt, one repository seam per hotspot. Days 60-90: extract first module (a low-churn, well-bounded domain), build a pilot vertical slice with the target architecture, publish the ADRs and a debt register. Beyond: strangle screen by screen, prioritized by churn x pain.
  7. Prevention: Architecture tests, PR template, quality gates (ANR/crash thresholds in release checklist), staged rollout with halt criteria.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No rewrite, no freeze, no framework fashion changes before observability exists. I'd accept ugly stable code. I'd say no to unscoped "quality" asks; convert to measurable goals (ANR < 1% in two quarters).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The CEO demands a rewrite timeline? → Show strangler plan with early wins and the risk of a 12-18 month zero-value rewrite.
  • The senior who wrote it resists? → Involve them as owner of the seam design; they hold domain knowledge.
  • Release takes 4 days? → Automate regression for top 10 journeys first.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite rescue started by fixing a SharedPreferences.commit() call in a hot path; the ANR rate fell from 3% to 1.4% in one release and bought credibility for the larger plan.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: rewrite-first.
  • Hire: observability, tests before refactor, strangler approach.
  • Strong hire: ties work to metrics and revenue, manages stakeholder expectations, grows the team's ownership.

questions.contextHtml: A seed-stage startup (6 Android devs, 40k DAU, shipping weekly) hired a contractor who built 38 Gradle modules, per-feature api/impl/di/testing submodules, a custom plugin system for navigation, and 9-layer mappers. Clean builds take 14 min (up from 5), incremental builds 90 s because of KAPT in 20 modules, and onboarding takes 3 weeks. Two feature PRs this month each touched 25+ files. The contractor argues "it will scale to 100 devs." The CEO plans to hire to 12 devs next year.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Delete modules to be simple" without data, or defend the contractor's design because "that's how big companies do it".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the actual hiring plan and timeline? Which modules change together? Where do builds spend time? Any module boundaries that map to real team ownership?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cheap build wins: enable build cache and configuration cache, move KAPT to KSP where supported, parallel execution.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Over-split modules cause configuration and KAPT overhead; (b) per-feature impl/di/testing splits that nobody else consumes are pure cost; (c) mapper chain adds PR width; (d) slow CI not module-related at all.
  4. How I'd verify: Gradle build scan and --profile, module dependency graph, co-change analysis from git (files that always change together should live together).
  5. Root cause: Architecture sized for a hypothetical 100-dev org, not the current 6 to 12.
  6. Fix: Merge modules that always change together (38 -> about 10), keep :core:* and a few feature modules where ownership is clear, drop api/impl splits with no second consumer, remove identical-shape mappers, keep the DI and navigation conventions. Document in an ADR with explicit revisit triggers (e.g. "split when two teams edit the same module weekly or clean build > 8 min").
  7. Prevention: Module-creation checklist (owner, reason, consumers), architecture review for new modules.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't flatten to a single module either: the build cache wins from some modularization are real. I'd accept that re-splitting later costs effort but is cheaper than paying every week now.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Contractor insists? → Debate with data (build scan, PR width); decisions need criteria, not authority.
  • 100 devs in 2 years? → Splits are reversible; add them when the org needs them.
  • Merge conflicts rise after merging? → Re-split along actual ownership lines.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team consolidated 40 modules to 12 and saw clean builds fall 14 -> 7 min while PR width halved; they re-extracted two modules a year later, when ownership split.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: pure opinion either way.
  • Hire: data-driven merge with revisit triggers.
  • Strong hire: separates reversible from irreversible choices, manages contractor and CEO conversation, quick wins first.

questions.promptHtml: How do you communicate an architecture trade-off to non-engineering stakeholders and to peers who disagree?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Staff-track engineers win decisions by framing, not by technical purity.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I state the decision in business outcomes, give two or three options with cost, risk and time, recommend one with a reason, and name what we're giving up. For peers, I write it as a short proposal (an ADR) with explicit criteria and invite counter-options before any meeting, so disagreement becomes about the criteria, not people.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Structure for stakeholders: Problem (in user/revenue terms) -> Options -> Recommendation -> Risk and mitigation -> Ask. Use numbers: "Option B delays the Q3 launch by 2 weeks but cuts crash rate 40% in checkout".

For peer disagreement: agree on decision criteria first (build time, testability, onboarding, risk, reversibility), score options, run a time-boxed spike if uncertain, "disagree and commit" with a written revisit date. Distinguish one-way doors (hard to reverse: persistence format, public API, module boundaries across teams) from two-way doors (UI library choice behind a seam): spend debate time proportional to irreversibility.

Proposal: Adopt Room over hand-written SQLite
Criteria: migration safety, test support, team familiarity, build cost
A Room (+KSP)   B SQLDelight   C status quo
Recommend A. Cost: 2 sprints. Revisit if KMP sharing becomes a goal.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: n/a (communication skill).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Jargon-first pitches ("we need MVI").
  • Presenting a single option as inevitable.
  • Winning the argument, losing the team (no ownership of outcome).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. PM says "no time for this"? → Offer a smaller slice with measurable payoff and the cost of delay in numbers.
  2. You lose the vote? → Commit, instrument the risk, record the revisit trigger.
  3. How do you handle a strong opinionated senior? → Shared criteria, spike data, and credit.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE argues technology. Senior argues outcomes, offers options, and makes disagreement decidable.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A migration proposal framed as "cuts release time from 4 days to 1" was funded in one meeting; the same proposal framed as "adopt clean architecture" had been rejected twice.

questions.contextHtml: A single-module app (12 devs, 280k lines, 1 :app module) has clean build 16 min, incremental build 3 min (any change recompiles most of the module), and daily merge conflicts in strings.xml, AppModule.kt and navigation graph files. CI has 140 runs/day. Management allows "one engineer, one quarter". A previous attempt split into :data, :ui, :models and made builds slower because everything depended on :models which changed constantly.
questions.promptHtml: How would you modularize incrementally and prove it worked?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Split by layers into :data/:domain/:ui." Repeats the failed attempt; layers change together on every feature, so there is no build isolation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which areas have most churn? Which features are well bounded? What's the target build time? Is there a design-system candidate for extraction? Who owns each feature?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Turn on build cache and configuration cache, set android.nonTransitiveRClass=true, move KAPT to KSP where possible; these often give gains without restructuring (verify with a build scan before and after).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Shared :models with an api leak, so any change recompiles all consumers (ABI churn); (b) layer modules coupled by every feature; (c) KAPT stubs dominate; (d) resources non-transitive R off.
  4. How I'd verify: Build scan (task timeline), --profile, ./gradlew :app:dependencies, module graph plugin, git co-change data.
  5. Root cause: Layer-based splitting plus wide api exposure caused the wrong coupling.
  6. Fix: Start with leaves that nothing depends on and that few things change: :core:designsystem, :core:network, then feature modules by domain with extraction order = lowest coupling first (e.g. Settings, About, then Search). Use implementation over api, feature modules depend on :core:* only, communicate through navigation contracts or :api modules. Define success: clean 16 -> under 8 min, incremental < 60 s, merge conflicts on shared files down.
  7. Prevention: Convention plugins for module setup, dependency rule checks, module-ownership file, build-time dashboard on CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No big-bang split, no layer modules. Accept extra boilerplate and navigation wiring as the price of isolation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A feature depends on 6 others? → Extract the shared abstraction into a core module or :api, otherwise leave it in :app for now.
  • Build isn't faster after extraction? → Check ABI changes and api leakage; non-incremental annotation processing.
  • Resource conflicts? → Prefix resources, enforce via lint.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team extracted 9 leaf features over a quarter; clean build 16 -> 9 min and shared-file conflicts dropped sharply, while the layered attempt had worsened both.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: layer split.
  • Hire: feature-first, leaves first, measures with build scans.
  • Strong hire: ABI/api awareness, success metrics, cheap non-structural wins first.

questions.contextHtml: Last Tuesday a rollout of a new navigation + DI structure (Navigation 2.8 type-safe routes, Hilt scoped ViewModels) reached 50% of 1.1M DAU. Crash-free sessions dropped from 99.4% to 97.9% within 3 hours; the top crash was java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Navigation destination that matches request NavDeepLinkRequest cannot be found from push-notification deep links created by the old server payload format. The alert fired at 98.5%, but nobody halted the staged rollout until 5 hours later; a rollback needed a new binary (store review: 18 hours). The remote flag only controlled analytics, not routing.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: causes, lessons, and changes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Developer forgot deep links; add a test." Blames a person and misses process, rollout, and architecture-level failures.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What was the exact timeline? Which versions and OS levels are affected? Were deep link formats documented anywhere? What did the rollout checklist include? Who had authority to halt?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the staged rollout, ship a hotfix that accepts both old and new link formats via a compatibility adapter, and use the server to temporarily emit the new payload shape.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Old payload routes not mapped in new graph; (b) cold-start vs warm-start intent handling difference; (c) process-death restoration; (d) red herring: Hilt scope change, which the stack trace doesn't support.
  4. How I'd verify: Stack traces by app version and entry point, replay captured notification payloads on a test device with adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d <uri>, compare nav graphs, review crash breakdown by source.
  5. Root cause: Migration changed a public contract (deep link URIs) with no compat layer, no automated deep-link regression suite, and a flag that did not guard the risky path.
  6. Fix: Short-term: hotfix compat adapter and halt gate. Long-term: treat deep links as a versioned public API with a contract test table of all known URIs; make the routing layer switchable by remote flag; define halt criteria (crash-free < 99.0% or delta > 0.3 pts at 10% halts automatically).
  7. Prevention: Blameless review, rollout runbook with named halt owner and automated guardrails, deep link instrumented test suite, canary at 1% for 24 h on each risky change.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Slower rollouts cost speed; accepted for high-risk changes only. I wouldn't ban architecture migrations or add a heavy approval gate for every PR.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Push payloads cached in the notification tray? → Old payloads outlive the binary; compat must remain for weeks.
  • Flag service failure? → Cached default must point to the stable path.
  • Whose fault? → The system's; fix guardrails.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite review discovered the alert fired correctly but routed to a channel nobody watched on weekends; changing the on-call route mattered more than any code fix.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames individual, adds one test.
  • Hire: timeline, causes at code and process level, rollout guardrails.
  • Strong hire: treats deep links as an API contract, versioning, automatic halt criteria, blameless framing.

questions.promptHtml: How do you decide which architecture decisions to make now and which to defer, and how do you keep an app evolvable?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who over-design from those who preserve options cheaply.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I sort decisions by cost of reversal. Hard-to-reverse ones (persisted data formats, public APIs and deep links, module boundaries across teams, auth/session model) get deliberate design and an ADR now. Easy-to-reverse ones (UI components, a library behind a seam, internal naming) I decide fast and move on. I keep evolvability by protecting seams, not by predicting the future.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
One-way vs two-way doors:

Hard to reverse (decide carefully)          Easy to reverse (decide fast)
- DB schema / serialized formats            - Image loader
- Deep link & API contracts                 - Internal mappers
- Module boundary between teams             - UI component library (behind theme)
- Auth/session & security model             - Logging backend

Techniques that preserve options: dependency inversion at boundaries, expand/contract schema changes, versioned contracts, feature flags with deletion dates, tests at boundaries rather than internals, and architecture tests (lint/Konsist) that keep dependency directions stable. Evolvability anti-patterns: speculative generality ("we might need plugin support"), framework leakage into domain code, and shared mutable singletons.

Revisit triggers: record in each ADR the measurable condition under which the decision should be reconsidered (team size, build time, MAU, new platform like KMP).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Cheap option-preserving seam: domain code never sees the persistence library
interface SessionStore { suspend fun read(): Session?; suspend fun write(s: Session) }
// Today: DataStore. Tomorrow: encrypted storage or KMP-shared. Callers unchanged.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Debating reversible choices for weeks.
  • Making irreversible choices (wire formats) casually.
  • "Future-proofing" with abstractions that never get a second implementation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. KMP in 2 years maybe? → Keep domain logic free of Android types; defer the actual move until a concrete need.
  2. How do you change a persisted format safely? → Expand/contract: write both, read new-then-old, backfill, then drop old.
  3. How do you know it's time to re-architect? → Revisit triggers from ADRs: lead time, incident rate, onboarding time.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE picks the "best" architecture up front. Senior spends rigor where reversal is expensive and keeps cheap exits elsewhere.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that stored serialized domain classes in SharedPreferences could not rename a field without breaking installed users; one that stored versioned DTOs migrated freely.
